analysis.one_liner: Taxes hedge funds on each single-family home they buy and on holding too many of them, forcing them to sell down their rental portfolios over a decade.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Finance Committee, where it has sat with no further action and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets large investment funds that buy up single-family houses and rent them out, which many economists say drives up home prices and squeezes out first-time buyers. It would charge a 15% tax every time a big fund buys a house, charge $5,000 per year for every house the fund holds above a shrinking cap (reaching zero after nine years), and take away those funds' mortgage-interest and depreciation tax breaks. Smaller landlords and owner-occupants are exempt. The bill has only six cosponsors, all from the Democratic side, and has not moved since being sent to the Senate Finance Committee in February 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary families trying to buy their first home. When large funds must shrink their stock of single-family houses or pay a growing tax, more homes come up for sale to individual buyers, reducing competition for the modest houses first-time buyers seek. Owner-occupants and small landlords are exempt.

how_it_helps.text: It puts an excise tax on large investment funds each time they buy a single-family home: the greater of 15% of the purchase price or $10,000, making each additional purchase more expensive.

It requires covered funds to sell down their stock of single-family homes over nine years — from 90% of their starting count down to zero for hedge funds — with a $5,000-per-home tax for every home held above the limit, and it counts sales to other businesses or to people who already own a home as non-sales so holdings cannot simply be shuffled.
It strips mortgage-interest and depreciation deductions from covered owners who remain over the limits, raising the cost of holding homes for profit rather than living in them.

analysis.who_pays: Hedge funds and other large pooled investors with $50 million or more in assets that own single-family homes, who would pay the purchase tax, per-home holding tax, and lost deductions — costs they could partly pass to their renters.

drawbacks.text: The tax could raise costs for renters: companies that own houses to rent them out might pass the new tax on in the form of higher rents on those homes.
The mandate to shrink foreclosure acquisitions could leave some vacant, foreclosed houses without a buyer and slow the recycling of abandoned properties back into use.

The tax applies only to certain large pooled-investment entities; other corporate and investor owners of single-family rentals are not covered, and large investors could restructure to fall outside the definitions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — pressuring large funds to sell off single-family homes so families can buy them — would be substantial in high-demand markets, and the multi-year phase-down gives funds time to sell without a crash. The drawbacks are real: the tax could be passed on to renters of fund-owned homes, the mandate on foreclosure sales could slow the handling of abandoned properties, and defining covered entities narrowly risks sophisticated workarounds. On balance it is a targeted, well-sequenced attempt at a genuine problem, though it addresses symptoms of housing scarcity rather than the underlying supply shortage.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has not taken it up, so it never moved toward a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 27, 2025 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Finance.
The Finance Committee has held no markup, hearing action, or floor vote on the bill, and it remains pending there.
It drew six cosponsors — two independents and four Democrats — and no Republican support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, large corporate landlords and funds that own single-family rental homes benefit from the inaction, since nothing has disturbed their holdings; prospective homebuyers have gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All six cosponsors are Democrats or independents aligned with Democrats and no Republican has signed on, but no vote has occurred, so the partisan shape of any eventual vote is unknown.

industries.industry: Institutional single-family rental owners and hedge funds
industries.note: The bill taxes new home purchases by large funds at 15% or $10,000 each, taxes holding homes above a shrinking cap at $5,000 each, and denies mortgage-interest and depreciation deductions. These firms' interest runs against prospective homebuyers: profits come from owning the entry-level housing stock families would otherwise buy.

industries.industry: Single-family rental operators below the $50 million threshold and non-fund investors
industries.note: Entities under the $50 million threshold, exempted construction/rehabilitation businesses, and nonprofits avoid the tax, so large competitors are disadvantaged relative to them. Non-fund individual buyers who already own a home are treated as disqualified transferees for counting purposes, but they face no tax themselves.

If funds sell off tens of thousands of homes to meet the declining caps, more houses come on the market for families to buy, easing competition and prices. Individual owner-occupants are exempt from the tax and are the preferred transferees under the counting rules.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Finance Committee with no action since its February 2025 referral and only six cosponsors, none from the Republican majority. Bills at this stage with this level of support almost never reach the floor; unless the committee acts, the bill is likely to die quietly at the end of the Congress.
